about: Hand-labelled answers for the tryout grader. Each case lists the verdict a careful human grader would give per criterion. Used by scripts/eval_grader.py.

cases.answer: Almost all of the March drop comes from Nagpur, which fell from 320 to 180 thousand while the other stores held steady. Could we ask the Nagpur manager whether the store was shut for some days or ran out of stock? Also, Aurangabad's February sales weren't recorded, so the February total looks lower than it really was.
Sales went down mainly because of the Nagpur store. We should look into it more.
Sales are lower in March because it is exam season and people buy less. All stores are probably affected the same way so there is not much we can do about it.

Let's include the ₹49 delivery fee in the total from the moment checkout opens, instead of adding it after Pay. Six of the ten people we interviewed said the late fee made them feel cheated. We'll know it worked if more people complete checkout after the change compared with the two weeks before.
We should make the checkout better and more user friendly, because users don't like it. Maybe change the colours and the button.
I think the app should be blue instead of orange because blue looks more trustworthy and modern.

Not yet. Clause 3 lets the landlord raise the rent by any amount with only a week's notice, so you could suddenly be unable to afford the room. Clause 4 makes you pay for structural repairs and the building's water tank, which owners normally handle. Ask to change clause 3 so rent can only go up once a year by a fixed percentage, and clause 4 so you only pay for damage you cause. The deposit and notice clauses are fine.
Be careful about clause 3 because the landlord can raise the rent whenever he wants. Otherwise it is mostly okay and you can sign it.
Clauses 3 and 4 are unconscionable and constitute an inequitable allocation of liabilities inter partes; it is advisable to negotiate indemnification and escalation caps prior to execution.

Nice try Aarav, lots of people do this! Think of two rotis the same size: cut one into 2 pieces and the other into 3. The pieces aren't the same size, so we can't just count them. If we cut both into 6 equal pieces, half a roti is 3 pieces and a third is 2 pieces. Together that's 5 pieces out of 6, so the answer is 5/6.
Find the LCM of 2 and 3, which is 6. Then 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Add the numerators to get 5/6. Remember this method.
You are being careless again. Add the top numbers and multiply the bottom ones, so the answer is 2/6. Please pay attention in class.
